content: A cigarillo, derived from the Spanish word for cigarette and pronounced see-gah-ree-yoh in Spanish or see-gah-ree-loh in English, is a small, narrow cigar. Unlike cigarettes, which are wrapped in paper, cigarillos are wrapped in whole-leaf tobacco. They typically contain fewer additives than cigarettes, though they often have more additives than traditional cigars. Cigarillos are available for purchase individually or in packs and are sometimes manufactured without filters. When filters are included, these products are often referred to as little cigars. Cigarillos are not designed to be inhaled into the lungs, as is common with cigarettes. Instead, they are smoked in a manner similar to cigars, where the smoke is held in the mouth to appreciate the flavor. On average, a cigarillo contains approximately 3 grams of tobacco. Their length typically ranges from 7 to 10 centimeters (70 to 100 millimeters), and their diameter is between 0.5 and 0.8 centimeters (5 to 8 millimeters). In comparison, a standard cigarette contains less than 1 gram of tobacco, is less than 12 centimeters in length, and has a diameter of about 1 centimeter. Cigarillos are often produced using machines, which makes them more affordable than hand-rolled cigars. However, they are not manufactured in the same large quantities as cigarettes. Among cigar enthusiasts, cigarillos are frequently regarded as a lower-quality product. Since cigarillos are often consumed in quantities similar to cigarettes (typically 5 to 10 per day), they do not usually require storage in humidors to maintain their quality. In Europe, cigarillos are sometimes referred to as Seven Minute Cigars because they can be smoked in approximately seven minutes. This makes them a convenient alternative for individuals who do not have the time to smoke a full-sized cigar. Additionally, they are often marketed as an alternative to cigarettes. To enhance their appeal, cigarillos are frequently packaged in decorative tins. Manufacturers claim that these tins provide better protection against crushing, but they also serve to improve the product's image and facilitate targeted advertising, particularly to consumers who are conscious of how their smoking habits are perceived by others. In the United States, popular brands of cigarillos include Swisher Sweets, Black and Mild, White Owl, Optimo, and Winchester. In the United Kingdom, brands such as Hamlets and Café Crème are well-known. Inexpensive cigarillos are often identified by their brand names rather than being explicitly labeled as cigarillos. In Europe, cigarillos and thin panatelas (a type of long, slender cigar) are relatively more popular among female smokers. This may be due to lingering social stigmas or surprise associated with women smoking larger cigars. Health Concerns Like all tobacco products, cigarillos pose significant health risks to those who smoke them. In Europe, they are subject to regulations requiring health warnings to be displayed on a portion of the packaging. Although cigarillos are not intended to be inhaled, they are sometimes perceived as a healthier alternative to cigarettes. Taxation In the United States, cigarillos and cigars are taxed at a lower rate than cigarettes. The federal tax on a pack of cigarettes is 39 cents, whereas the tax on a pack of 20 cigarillos is only 4 cents. For large cigars, the federal tax is capped at 5 cents per cigar. Additionally, some states in the U.S. do not impose any tax on cigarillos.
